sections.h2: Where is Jacksonville, Arkansas, and what kind of city is it?
sections.html:
Jacksonville is a city in Pulaski County, about 17 miles northeast of Little Rock, and it belongs to the Little Rock-North Little Rock-Conway metropolitan area. It sits at roughly 300 feet above sea level and has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and mostly mild to cool winters.

The Census Bureau counted 29,477 residents in 2020 and estimates 29,460 for 2025, so the city has been close to 30,000 people for about three decades. That steadiness matters if you plan to sell a house here: the buyer pool is mostly local households, air base families and people who work elsewhere in the Little Rock area.

The jump from 2,474 to 14,488 residents in a single decade tells most of the story of the city's housing stock. That growth came right as the air base opened in the mid-1950s, so a good part of the city's housing is likely to date from those years.

sections.h2: How did Jacksonville start, and why does that history matter to a house sale?
sections.html:
Jacksonville began as a railroad depot settlement in 1870. It is named for Nicholas Jackson, a landowner who deeded right-of-way land to the Cairo and Fulton Railroad that year, and it was incorporated in 1941.

The same year, construction began on the Arkansas Ordnance Plant, where fuses and detonators were developed for World War II. When the war ended the plant closed and its land was sold for commercial use, including the land for Little Rock Air Force Base in 1955. The plant's guard house is on the National Register of Historic Places, and the Jacksonville Museum of Military History preserves part of the story.

For a seller, the practical point is age. Houses built in the decades after the air base opened are now well past fifty years old, so buyers and inspectors tend to look closely at roofs, older wiring, plumbing and foundations. A house that needs that kind of work is a common reason owners here look at an as-is sale.

sections.h2: How does Little Rock Air Force Base shape the Jacksonville housing market?
sections.html:
The base is the largest single influence on local demand. Little Rock Air Force Base lies in Jacksonville, covers 6,217 acres and is described as the primary C-130 training base for the Department of Defense.

Its host unit is the 19th Airlift Wing, and several associate units share the base, including the 314th Airlift Wing, the Arkansas Air National Guard's 189th Airlift Wing and the Air Force Reserve's 913th Airlift Group. The base reports a resident population of more than 3,300 and a working population of about 7,200, and it is the fourth-largest employer in Arkansas, with a stated local economic impact of $813.6 million.

  • Training crews and permanent personnel create steady rental and purchase demand.
  • Reassignments (permanent change of station orders) can force a sale on a short timeline.
  • Military owners who move away often become landlords or sell with a tenant still in place.

If you are a service member or a family handling a quick move, the speed and certainty of a cash sale can matter more than squeezing out the highest list price.

sections.h2: What is the AICUZ overlay, and does it affect selling a Jacksonville house?
sections.html:
The AICUZ overlay is a Jacksonville zoning district that applies land-use limits around the air base, and it can affect houses near the flight paths. Jacksonville adopted it by ordinance in 1999 under Arkansas Act 530 of 1995, using the Air Installation Compatible Use Zone study for the base.

The overlay covers the Clear Zone and Accident Potential Zones I and II, inside and outside city limits within the city's planning jurisdiction. According to the city code, residential development in the affected area is limited to one single-family dwelling per acre, uses may not expose people to noise above DNL 75 dB, and construction must follow sound-insulation provisions. Existing uses generally continue, and a structure rebuilt after damage can stay if its main use does not change.

The city clerk files a certified copy of the ordinance with the Pulaski County Circuit Clerk, Real Estate Division, and that filing serves as official notice to current and future owners, title insurers and lenders. If your house is close to the base, ask a title company or the city's planning staff whether the overlay touches your lot before you set a timeline.

sections.h2: What did the March 2023 tornado do in Jacksonville?
sections.html:
The EF3 tornado of March 31, 2023, crossed Jacksonville after moving through west Little Rock, North Little Rock and Sherwood. The National Weather Service rated it EF3 with peak winds of 165 mph, and it ran about 34 miles before weakening near Cabot.

In Jacksonville the damage included Dupree Park and the First Assembly of God Church. The Weather Service lists west Little Rock, Jacksonville and Burns Park in North Little Rock among the areas with significant damage, with at least 2,700 structures affected overall.

Storm history shapes what sellers face. Roofs patched after a storm, insurance claims that were never closed out, and permits that were never finalized are all things a buyer's lender or inspector can find. A cash buyer who accepts the house as-is can sidestep many of these questions, although you should still be ready to disclose known damage.

sections.h2: What does the housing stock look like in Jacksonville?
sections.html:
The 2020 census recorded 12,738 housing units in Jacksonville, with 10.1 percent of them vacant. The homeowner vacancy rate was 2.2 percent and the rental vacancy rate was 10.5 percent.

A low homeowner vacancy rate next to a higher rental vacancy rate suggests that owner-occupied homes tend to be occupied while rentals turn over more often. Landlords holding a vacant Jacksonville rental should keep that gap in mind.

Jacksonville is served by the Jacksonville North Pulaski School District. The city was part of the Pulaski County Special School District from 1927 until voters approved leaving it on September 16, 2014, by 3,672 votes to 202. The new district became fully independent on July 1, 2016.

The district runs six elementary schools, Jacksonville Middle School and Jacksonville High School. Arkansas State University-Beebe also operates a degree center at the air base. Buyers with children usually ask which school zone a house falls in, so keep that answer handy when you talk to anyone about your listing.

sections.h2: What parks and amenities do Jacksonville buyers ask about?
sections.html:
The city lists eight parks: Dupree, Fireman, Excell, Galloway, Johnson, Paradise, Northlake and Stagecoach. Other draws include the Bayou Meto Urban Canoe Trail, the Arkansas Game and Fish Foundation Shooting Sports Complex, Reed's Bridge Battlefield Heritage Park, a farmers market and the Esther DeWitt Nixon Library, which belongs to the Central Arkansas Library System.

Jacksonville is classed as a moist city for alcohol sales: stores cannot sell it, but some restaurants can serve it with special permits. That rarely changes a home's value, but it is one of the local rules newcomers sometimes ask about.

sections.h2: How do property taxes and recording work when you sell in Jacksonville?
sections.html:
Pulaski County bills the property tax, and Arkansas collectors take payments from the first business day of March through October 15 of the year after assessment. Taxes unpaid after October 15 carry a 10 percent penalty, and the Arkansas portal for property tax payments points Pulaski County owners to the county treasurer's public site.

  • Assessors generally compute tax on 20 percent of market value, and the taxable value of a homestead can rise only 5 percent a year until it reaches full assessed value.
  • Counties reappraise on four-year cycles under Act 139 of 2023.
  • A substantive appeal must be scheduled with the county board of equalization by the third Monday in August.

The state's real property transfer tax is $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on deeds over $100. Deeds for Jacksonville property are recorded with the Pulaski Circuit and County Clerk, Real Estate Department, at 401 West Markham Street in Little Rock. The clerk charges $15 for the first page and $5 for each added page, and since August 5, 2025, filers who are not attorneys, brokers, lenders or government representatives need a photo ID.

sections.h2: What are your options for selling a house in Jacksonville?
sections.html:
You can list with an agent, sell it yourself, or accept a cash offer. Listing works best when the house is in good shape and you can wait through showings, inspections and a buyer's loan approval. A cash sale trades some of that upside for speed and fewer conditions.

  • Tenants in place: a cash buyer can often take the house with the lease intact.
  • Inherited house: check who holds title and whether probate must be finished first.
  • Behind on payments: ask your lender for a payoff figure before any offer so you know what the sale must cover.
  • Storm or age-related repairs: an as-is sale avoids a repair list.

faqs.q: How many people live in Jacksonville, Arkansas?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau estimates 29,460 residents as of 2025, down very slightly from 29,477 counted in the 2020 census.

faqs.q: Does Little Rock Air Force Base affect home values in Jacksonville?
faqs.a: It affects demand and some land-use rules. The base is the fourth-largest employer in Arkansas, and the city's AICUZ overlay limits development in the zones near the base. Ask a title company whether your lot falls inside the overlay.

faqs.q: Which county do I deal with when I sell a house in Jacksonville?
faqs.a: Pulaski County. Property taxes are billed through the county, and deeds are recorded at the Pulaski Circuit and County Clerk's Real Estate Department in Little Rock.

faqs.q: When are Arkansas property taxes due, and what happens if they are late?
faqs.a: They are due by October 15 of the year after assessment, and unpaid taxes carry a 10 percent penalty. Delinquent real estate taxes also accrue interest, so confirm the payoff amount with the county before closing.

faqs.q: Was Jacksonville hit by the 2023 tornado?
faqs.a: Yes. The March 31, 2023, EF3 tornado crossed Jacksonville and damaged Dupree Park and a church. Houses with storm damage can still be sold as-is.
